extracted.intended_audience: analysts and rulewriters at Federal executive agencies and establishments (heads of agencies, regulatory analysts preparing regulatory analyses)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing regulatory analyses for major Federal rulemakings, including what to measure, how to measure benefits and costs, what alternatives to consider, and specialized analytic requirements under statute and Executive Orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key elements of a regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good regulatory analysis should include the following three basic elements: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives identified by the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate properly the benefits and costs you must: explain how actions required by the rule are linked to expected benefits; identify a baseline (normally 'no action'); identify expected undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits; assess quantitatively when possible; include discussion of non-quantified effects; present a summary of benefit and cost estimates for each alternative including qualitative/non-monetized factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain linkage between actions and expected benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the actions required by the rule are linked to the expected benefits. For example, indicate how additional safety equipment will reduce safety risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do a similar linkage analysis for each alternative; show causal pathways from regulatory provisions to outcomes so benefit estimates are traceable to required actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and state a baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a baseline. Benefits and costs are defined in comparison with a clearly stated alternative, normally a 'no action' baseline: what the world will be like if the proposed rule is not adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons to a 'next best' alternative are also useful; clearly state what baseline is used for all incremental estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify ancillary effects and side‑effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the expected undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits of the proposed regulatory action and the alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add these to direct benefits and costs as appropriate and discuss their magnitude and importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non‑quantified as well as quantified benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete regulatory analysis includes a discussion of non-quantified as well as quantified benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When non-quantified outcomes are important, carry out threshold (break-even) analysis, indicate which non-quantified effects are most important and why, and explain how they could change the ranking of alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation with affected parties and experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek out the opinions of those who will be affected by the regulation as well as the views of individuals and organizations with special knowledge or insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation can provide relevant data and should not be limited to the final stages; early consultation is especially helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of professional judgment and tailored analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Conducting high-quality analysis requires competent professional judgment; different regulations may call for different emphases in the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single formula; balance thoroughness with practical analytical capacity and focus the analysis where sensitivity and complexity warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of assumptions, methods, and data
rubrics_metrics.description: A good analysis is transparent. It should be possible for a qualified third party to see clearly how estimates and conclusions were derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State assumptions (time horizon, discount rates, etc.), provide sensitivity analysis, specific references to all data sources, appendices documenting models, results of uncertainty analyses, an executive summary, and a standardized accounting statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate need for Federal regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending Federal regulatory action, an agency must demonstrate that the proposed action is necessary and identify statutory authority and extent of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the problem to be addressed, assess its significance, describe market failures or other compelling public needs qualitatively and (where feasible) quantitatively, and show government intervention is likely to do more good than harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and document market failures or other social purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: When regulation is intended to correct a market failure or serve another social purpose, the analysis should describe the failure and justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major types of market failure to consider include externalities/common property/public goods, market power, and inadequate or asymmetric information; other justifications include government efficiency, redistribution, anti‑discrimination, privacy, and similar objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative non‑regulatory means and appropriate governmental level
rubrics_metrics.description: Before federal regulation, consider other means (antitrust, litigation, compensation systems) and whether State/local regulation or Federal action is most appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine state/local discretion, potential gains from regulatory experimentation, costs of fragmented regulation, and international harmonization/trade effects (non‑tariff barriers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against certain types of economic regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption against certain regulatory actions; a particularly demanding burden of proof is required to demonstrate the need for: price controls in competitive markets; production or sales quotas; mandatory uniform quality standards if voluntary standards or disclosure suffice; and controls on entry into employment or production (with limited exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document strong justification when proposing such regulations and explain statutory or compelling reasons for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider an array of alternative regulatory approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider a range of alternatives and explore modifications of some or all of a regulation's attributes to identify appropriate options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a manageable number of reasonable alternatives for detailed analysis, balancing thoroughness and practicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine different statutory choices available
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute establishes a specific requirement and the agency is considering a more stringent standard, examine benefits and costs of reasonable alternatives that reflect the range of statutory discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze alternatives that are within the legal discretion provided by statute, including the specific statutory requirement as one alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate different compliance dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider different timing options because compliance dates can materially affect net benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lead times and implementation schedules; delayed implementation can reduce costs or, in some cases, produce losses of future benefits—analyze tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider different enforcement methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and evaluate alternative compliance and enforcement frameworks (on-site inspections, periodic reporting, penalties, random monitoring, parametric monitoring, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose enforcement methods that provide appropriate incentives at least cost; consider federal/state/local enforcement mixes and monitoring costs versus effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider different degrees of stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: Study alternative levels of regulatory stringency to understand how benefits, costs, and their distribution vary with stringency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze marginal benefits and costs across stringency levels and study incremental effects to identify efficient tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider differential requirements by firm size
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider setting different regulatory requirements for large and small firms based on estimated differences in compliance costs or benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for Regulatory Flexibility Act implications; small firms may face higher per-unit costs—assess efficiency and equity consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider geographic differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider different requirements for different geographic regions when benefits and costs vary regionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess regional heterogeneity in benefits and costs and the administrative feasibility of geographically varying rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer performance standards to design standards when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance standards (outcome-based) are generally superior because they give regulated parties flexibility to achieve objectives cost‑effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for compliance cost savings from flexibility and the costs of assuring compliance (monitoring, measurement); weigh tradeoffs when choosing between performance and design standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider market‑oriented approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore market-oriented alternatives (fees, penalties, subsidies, marketable permits/offsets, changes in liability/property rights, mandated bonds/insurance) rather than direct controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include averaging/banking/trading (ABT) for emissions; evaluate cost reduction potential and distributional/local effects (hot spots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider informational measures where information failures exist
rubrics_metrics.description: If inadequate or asymmetric information is the problem, consider informational remedies (standardized testing/rating systems, mandatory disclosure, government provision of information) instead of product standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate costs (gathering/communicating info, displaced info) and perverse incentives; prefer least intrusive informational measure sufficient to accomplish the objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Benefit‑Cost Analysis (BCA) appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: BCA expresses both benefits and costs in monetary units and is the framework for identifying the most efficient alternative (largest net benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure incremental benefits and costs of successively more stringent alternatives; do not rely on benefit‑cost ratios alone to infer net benefits; when monetization is impossible, measure physical units or describe qualitatively and use threshold analysis for non‑quantified factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cost‑Effectiveness Analysis (CEA) appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: CEA compares regulatory options when the primary benefits are health/safety improvements or when benefits cannot all be monetized but a validity effectiveness measure exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare CEA for major health/safety rulemakings with valid effectiveness measures; for other major rulemakings perform BCA and CEA as appropriate; prefer final outcomes (lives saved, life‑years) over intermediate outputs; use incremental CEA and eliminate dominated alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: CEA: construct costs and effectiveness measures carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When doing CEA, construct the numerator (net costs) to include all relevant societal costs and subtract monetized ancillary benefits; construct the denominator using appropriate effectiveness measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double-counting, choose final outcome measures, capture variability in quality of outcomes (e.g., ecological value of wetlands), explain choice of effectiveness metric, and be cautious interpreting average cost‑effectiveness ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness metrics for public health and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Use measures such as lives saved, life‑years saved, equivalent lives (ELs), or quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) where appropriate and consider morbidity as well as mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrated measures capture morbidity and mortality but rest on restrictive preference assumptions; consider including at least one integrated measure when both mortality and morbidity matter; account for fairness across population segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of benefits and costs over time and discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Present undiscounted streams of annual benefits and costs for each year of the analytic time horizon and present annualized benefits and costs using real discount rates of 3 percent and 7 percent; report monetized effects in 2001 dollars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin streams in the first year the final rule has effects; convert dollars from other years using the GDP deflator; present alternative estimates where mortality valuations differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of risk and uncertainty and sensitivity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates and distributions where available; include sensitivity analyses for key assumptions and alternative assumptions when estimates depend heavily on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When only bounds are provided, use 95 and 5 percent confidence bounds if possible; disclose plausible alternative assumptions and show whether rankings change; assume risk neutrality in general unless justified otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting statement and reporting categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accounting statement with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates for each major final rule and report estimates within three categories: monetized, quantified but not monetized, and qualitative but not quantified or monetized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive; avoid double‑counting; present precision, footnotes, and documentation; include an executive summary and use suggested formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifying, monetizing, and precision of estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop quantitative estimates and convert them to dollar amounts where possible; reported estimates should reflect precision in the analysis (rounding should reflect implied precision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $220 million implies rounding to nearest $10 million (+/- $5 million); $222 million implies rounding to nearest $1 million (+/- $0.5 million).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate reporting of transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Report transfer payments separately and avoid misclassifying transfers as benefits or costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish transfers caused by Federal budget actions from transfers between non‑governmental parties; use categories needed to describe redistributive effects; identify transfers that also have efficiency effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify distributional effects (state/local/tribal, small business, wages, growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of benefits, costs, and transfers received by State, local, and tribal governments and, to the extent feasible, effects on small businesses, wages, and economic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that rules with annual costs under $1 billion are likely to have minimal effect on economic growth; comply with Regulatory Flexibility Act when impacts on small entities are significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized statutory and EO analytical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider specialized analyses required by law or Executive Orders, including Regulatory Flexibility Act (impact on small entities), Unfunded Mandates Act (written statement for >$100 million aggregate expenditures), Paperwork Reduction Act (information collection approval), Information Quality Guidelines, NEPA (EIS), EO 13045 (children's health/safety), EO 13211 (energy impacts), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure applicable statutory thresholds are checked, prepare required statements/forms, consult agency counsel and OMB where appropriate, and post RFCAs or other analyses online when useful.
